title: Arepas
subtitle: colombian and venezuelan corn flatbreads
excerpt: Thick, tender corn flatbreads eaten at breakfast, lunch and dinner across Colombia and Venezuela. Cooked on a griddle until golden on both sides with a soft, chewy centre.
sourceNotes: Arepas are made from pre-cooked white maize flour (masarepa), which is different from regular cornmeal or polenta. The dough comes together in minutes and needs no resting time.

recipe.freezeNotes: Cook completely, cool, then freeze in layers separated by baking paper. Reheat in a dry pan or low oven.
recipe.batchNotes: Makes 8 arepas easily. Double the quantities for a larger batch.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The dough can rest for up to 30 minutes before shaping. Cook on the day.

glossaryTerms.definition: A thick corn flatbread eaten daily in Colombia and Venezuela, stuffed or eaten plain.

content.text: are made from masarepa, a pre-cooked white maize flour that hydrates quickly into a soft, pliable dough. The whole process from mixing to eating takes under 30 minutes. They are eaten plain, stuffed with cheese or beans, or served alongside soups and stews.
The dough should feel like soft Play-Doh. If it cracks at the edges when you press a disc flat, add water a tablespoon at a time until it holds together smoothly.

items.prepNote: pre-cooked white maize flour, such as masarepa

content.text: Pour the lukewarm water into a large bowl. Add the masarepa flour and the melted butter if using. Mix with your hands until a smooth, soft dough forms. It should not stick to your hands. If it cracks when pressed, add a little more water.
Divide the dough into 8 equal balls. Roll each ball between your palms until smooth, then press flat into a disc about 1.5 cm thick and 9 cm across. Smooth any cracks at the edge.
Heat a dry frying pan or griddle pan over medium heat. No oil is needed.
Cook the arepas for 5 minutes per side. They should develop a dry, golden-brown crust. Turn and cook the other side. The sound will change from sizzling to a dull knock when they are ready.
The inside should be soft and slightly chewy. Eat immediately, split and filled, or serve whole alongside stews. They cool quickly, so serve straight from the pan.

attrs.issue: Arepas are raw in the middle after 10 minutes

content.text: They are too thick. Press each disc to no more than 1.5 cm. Alternatively, finish them in a 180C oven for 8 minutes after browning both sides.

attrs.issue: Dough is cracking and hard to shape

content.text: The dough is too dry. Add lukewarm water, one tablespoon at a time, and knead briefly until it becomes pliable. Masarepa absorbs water differently between brands.

attrs.issue: Arepas are sticking to the dry pan

content.text: Do not move them before a crust forms. They will release naturally once the underside is golden. If they stick, add a very thin layer of oil to the pan.

Arepas have been eaten in Colombia and Venezuela for thousands of years. Indigenous communities made them before European contact using ground maize. Today they are eaten at every meal of the day. Colombian arepas tend to be thinner and plainly seasoned. Venezuelan arepas are thicker and typically stuffed. The two countries consider them a point of national pride and friendly rivalry.
